books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, B. Cotton, Slavery, and the Southern Exception

stimulus.text:
Enslaved people counted in the United States, by census year:

| Census year | Enslaved people |
|---|---|
| 1790 | 697,681 |
| 1800 | 893,602 |
| 1820 | 1,538,022 |
| 1840 | 2,487,355 |

Source: United States census counts, 1790–1840.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the United States census counts, 1790–1840, as carried by the Historical Census Browser; checked against Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 B (about 700,000 in 1790; 2 million by 1830).

source: original; data table from United States census counts, 1790–1840
stem: The table shows the enslaved population more than doubling between 1800 and 1840. Which development most directly explains that growth?

options.text: The reopening of the Atlantic slave trade by Congress in 1808
options.misconception: Congress banned the importation of enslaved people in 1808; it did not reopen the trade.

options.text: The spread of factory wage labor in Southern cities
options.misconception: The South stayed farm-based in this period; factory wage labor grew in the North.

options.text: The cotton gin, which made short-staple cotton profitable
The end of slavery in the northern states, which freed enslaved people to move south
options.misconception: Northern emancipation freed few people, and it did not send them south as enslaved labor.

rationales.A: Congress banned the importation of enslaved people in 1808. It did not reopen the trade.
rationales.B: The South stayed farm-based in this period. Factory wage labor grew in the North.
rationales.C: The cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable, planters grew far more cotton, and cotton farming needed enslaved labor.
rationales.D: Northern emancipation freed few people, and it did not send them south as enslaved labor.
rationales.general:
1. Read the table. The enslaved population rose from about 894,000 in 1800 to about 2,487,000 in 1840.
2. Ask what changed in those years. The cotton gin made short-staple cotton profitable, and cotton spread across the South.
3. Link the two. Cotton farming needed many hands, so planters bought more enslaved workers.
Background: Congress banned importing enslaved people in 1808, so this growth came from natural increase and the domestic slave trade.
Remember: when two trends rise together, ask which one drives the other.
